title: Chapter 125 – The House Asks Again
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

They bury Sang Ruo on the ridge above the Sutra Hall, in the cold, with no bell.

It is the way she asked. No chant, no procession of robed elders, no paper money. Ye has chosen the place herself, a flat shelf of rock under a crooked pine, from which the whole valley can be seen on a clear day: the terraces, the Garden, the long gray road down to the plain. Four men carry the plain coffin. Qin Hao is one of them, and he carries his corner on the flat of his forearm, because he cannot close a stone hand around the handle.

Jian stands at the back with his hood up and his hands folded in his sleeves.

There are perhaps forty people on the shelf. The clerks of the Sutra Hall, in a dark, awkward row. A dozen Numbers who have not yet been told, and who came only because they were asked. Wenyuan and Qinghe, side by side, with Yue between them and Pebble at her heel. Bai, bent over his stick. Kuang, in his fresh Inner Sect sash, pretending he is not crying. And Ye, in front of them all, leaning on her black stick with both hands, her face a stone mask.

She does not make a speech. When the coffin is down, she says one word in the oldest script, the hooked character, and every clerk in the Sutra Hall bows their head, because every one of them was taught to write it by the woman in the box.

Remain.

Then she picks up a handful of earth, lets it fall, and walks away down the slope without looking back.

* * *

Jian waits until the shelf is empty.

The wind is rising. Somewhere below, a bell is ringing for the evening meal, the ordinary bell, and the sound is thin and bright and wrong in the cold. He crouches by the new mound and puts his hand flat on the cold earth, as he once put it on the Gate, and does not know what he is looking for.

He finds it anyway.

It is a small, dull ache, behind his breastbone, in the place where the Cole door sits. It has been there since the day the door opened. It is not pain. It is closer to a pressure, a sense of a name on the tip of the tongue, and for three nights now it has grown steadily stronger. He has told himself that it is the strain of the Seal, still raw and slowly mending. He has told himself that it is grief.

It is neither. It is a hand on his shoulder.

"I know," he says aloud, to nobody. "I felt it."

There is no answer. But the pressure shifts, a little, like a sleeper turning over, and he understands with perfect and unwelcome clarity that something very large, a long way down, has just noticed that he has noticed.

* * *

Ye finds him at midnight, at the foot of the Dock stair, with a book in her hands.

She has not slept. He can see it in the set of her mouth. She stands in the green glow of the Gate wall in her black robe with the stick under one arm and the Roll cradled against her chest like a sleeping infant, and she does not say good evening.

"It will not close," she says.

"The Roll?"

"The last page. I have tried everything. I have put it in a chest. I have put the chest in the stacks. I have carried it to the Gate and back." Her voice is flat. "Each time I open the cover, it is on the last page, and your name is on the last line, and the ink is wet."

She holds it out. Jian looks at the cloth cover, plum-colored, worn at the corners, and at the pale hands that have held it for fifty-five years without ever once opening it, until three days ago.

"Do not hand it to me," he says.

"Why not?"

"Because if I take it, I think it will be true."

Ye looks at him for a long moment. "It is already true," she says. "Whether you touch it or not." She sets the Roll down on the lowest step, gently, as one sets down a covered dish. "That is what I came to tell you. I am old, and I am not clever, but I have read the Rule of the Keepers a thousand times, and there is a clause that nobody talks about. A Keeper is not appointed by a vote. A Keeper is recognized. The Roll writes the name of the person the House already holds, whether that person knows it or not."

"I have never been held by the House."

"No?" Her eyes are very sharp. "Four times they tried to buy you. Twice they sent a seat. The Registry marked you before you were born, Sang Ruo told me, and the House watched you for thirty-five years from behind a wall. Whatever else you may be, Lin Jian, you have been held. You simply did not feel the hand."

He says nothing. Behind his breastbone the pressure turns over again, patient and enormous.

"Read the page," says Ye. "Please. I cannot bear to see your name there and not know what it means."

* * *

He picks up the Roll. It is heavier than a book should be.

The cover is cold, like a stone from the bottom of a well. When he opens it, the pages part by themselves, and he sees, in a plum-colored script that he can read without trying, line after line of names descending the left margin, thirty-one of them, each with a date, each in a different hand. The last is Sang Ruo. It is crossed out with a single clean stroke, the stroke of someone closing a ledger. Beneath it, in letters that glisten, is his own name, and beneath his name, in a small, neat, formal hand, a single line:

Keeper, by the will of the House. Entry pending your answer.

"Pending," Ye whispers.

"It is asking," says Jian.

"It cannot ask. It has no mouth. Sang Ruo burned the mouth."

"Then something else is speaking for it."

The page begins to glow.

It is not the green glow of the Gate. It is the dim, warm, dusty violet of old sleep. Jian feels it first in his teeth, then in the soles of his feet, and then the air in the Dock stair shifts and thickens, and the lamp on the wall gutters, and he hears, not in his ears but somewhere behind his eyes, the sound of breathing.

Many people. Slowly. In the same rhythm.

Thirty-one.

* * *

Keeper, says a voice.

It is not one voice. It is thirty-one voices, laid on top of each other so exactly that they sound like one: a man's, a woman's, an old one, a young one, a child's, a bass that shakes the floor. It does not shout. It speaks in the courteous, dry, level tone of a long-serving clerk presenting a very reasonable account.

Keeper. We ask your pardon for the manner of the asking.

Ye has gone gray. She grips the stair rail. Jian does not move.

"Who speaks?"

The Sleepers of the Chain. The ones who hold the House's breath, since the Roll has no Keeper to hold it. We are not the House. We are the House's habit. It is a small difference. We have found that it is the one that matters.

"Is the Sect Head with you?"

He is the first of us. He sleeps at the head of the Chain, and has slept for forty-one years, and what he dreams is the House. The voice softens by a hair. We do not wish him harm. We wish only to be released. We were promised, when we lay down, that the sleeping would last a season. It has lasted a lifetime.

Jian breathes out slowly. "What do you want?"

A very little. A thing you were already inclined to do. The thirty-one voices pause, all together, like singers drawing breath. There is a stone on your shelf. It is the third of three. It has your name on its seam. If you will seat it, in the Dock that you built in your soul, we will wake.

"You will wake."

All of us. The Head first. He will open his eyes in his bed, and he will remember his name, and he will be old, and weak, and himself. A pause. The Chain will break. Thirty-one will be released. The breath we have been drawing from them for forty years will return. The House will lose its last holdings. This is an honest offer, Keeper. There is no trick in it that we can see.

"There is always a trick."

Always, the voices agree, with a faint and terrible humor. We cannot see this one. We can only tell you what it costs us. It costs us everything. And we ask it freely.

* * *

Jian is silent for a long moment.

Beside him, Ye is breathing hard. Behind them the Gate wall pulses green, steady as a heart. And in the pocket of his cloak, beneath his hand, a small, cold, heavy stone lies against his palm like the pebble in a sling.

"Why should fragment three wake you?" he asks.

It does not wake us. It releases the Chain. The three stones were made together; the first holds the Gate's lock, the second holds its key, the third holds its door. When the three sit together, the Chain has nothing to hold on to. The voice almost sounds apologetic. We were made with a design flaw. We are held to the Dock by a rope that was meant to be cut.

"Cut by whom?"

By the Operator. By the eighth.

Silence.

"Say that again."

By the eighth, Keeper. By you. The Chain was built to wait for the eighth. It was told, in the beginning, that when the eighth Operator came and seated the third stone, the waiting would be over and the sleepers would wake and the House could rest. The voices drop to a whisper. We have waited six hundred years for you to do what you are about to do. Please do it.

Ye makes a small sound.

Jian lifts his head and looks at her. He sees in her face the same thing he feels in his own: not triumph, not relief, but the cold prickle of a very old trap, so old and so patient that it has stopped looking like one.

"If I seat the third stone," he says, "what else happens?"

Nothing.

"Nothing."

Nothing that we know.

He lets the silence stretch. Then he asks, very quietly, the question he has been holding since he first opened the Roll.

"And if I do not?"

* * *

There is a long pause. When the voices answer, the courtesy is gone from them.

Then we sleep, they say. And we are drained, as we are always drained, a little each season, by the House's habit and the Gate's hunger. The Chain was built with thirty-one links. One by one, they fail. We have lost four in forty years.

"Four."

We name them. Lo Banxia, who was nineteen. Tuo Fei, who could sing. Old Sun. A girl we never knew the name of. The thirty-one voices are quite steady. The weakest of us now is the ninth, who has perhaps twenty years in her. After her, the eleventh. After that, the Head himself. We would not have you do this for us. We have no right. We ask only that you know it.

"Twenty years."

Or nineteen. We are not precise.

Ye is staring at the floor. Her knuckles are white on the stair rail. Jian looks at the glowing book, at the line of wet ink that bears his name, and feels the weight of thirty-one sleeping faces pressing against the inside of his eyes. It is a weight he knows. It is the weight of the Orchard roll, of the Ironwood wardens, of every name he has ever been unable to save. He has spent thirty-six years learning to carry it. He had hoped he would learn to put it down.

He reads it twice. Then he closes the panel, as a man shuts a book on a bad page, and looks at the Roll.

"You say there is no trick."

We say we cannot see one.

"A thing built to wait six hundred years for a man to do one small thing is a thing that wants it done."

That is true.

"Then I want to know who it is that wants it."

The voices are silent. A long, deep, uncertain silence, like a man at the bottom of a stair who has been asked the wrong question. And then, so faintly that Jian might have imagined it, one voice among the thirty-one speaks apart from the rest. A woman's voice, the voice of someone very tired and very old, with the dry precision of a lifelong clerk.

We would tell you, Keeper, it says. If we knew.

* * *

He does not answer that night.

He closes the book, gently, and the voices fall silent, and the violet glow fades from the page. He hands the Roll back to Ye with both hands and tells her to keep it in the stick, where it was safe for fifty-five years. She does not argue. She puts it in the hollow, screws the stopper tight, and stands there in the Gate's green light with her face in her hands.

"They are people," she says. "Asleep. Dreaming. Four of them dead and nobody told."

"I know."

"Twenty years."

"I know."

"And you will not do it."

Jian looks at the Gate wall. It stands as it has always stood, a slab of dark green stone older than the Sect, humming faintly to itself. Qin Hao's hand-marks are still on its surface, two shallow prints where he sealed it with his body. Jian puts his own palm over one of them, and it is warm.

"I will not do it tonight," he says.

"That is not an answer."

"It is the only one I have." He takes his hand away. "I do not know who built the third stone, Ye. I do not know why it was made to be seated by the eighth. I know that the first stone gave me a Reservoir, and the second gave me a Door, and each time the price was something I did not see coming. If this one is worth thirty-one lives, it may be worth more than I can pay."

"And if it is a trap?"

"Then someone has spent six hundred years setting it, and I would like to look at the bait before I bite."

She studies him. She is a hundred years old almost, and she has buried a teacher this week, and her eyes in the green light are as hard and clear as winter water.

"You are very like her," she says at last. "She also thought that the right thing to do was to refuse and wait."

"Did she regret it?"

"Every day." Ye picks up her stick. "But she never once thought she was wrong."

* * *

Qin Hao is waiting at the top of the stair, in the dark.

He stands with his back against the wall and his stone hands hanging at his sides, a big man gone gray, with a face that has not slept either. He has been listening, Jian realizes. He heard the last of it.

"You said eighth," says Qin Hao.

"Yes."

"The Roll said eight Operators. All of them Cole."

"All of them."

"And you are the eighth." He says it slowly. "Which means the other seven did what? Went through the Gate and—" He stops. "Did not come back."

"I do not know."

"Do you want to?"

Jian looks at the older man's face, at the blunt, weathered, loyal features that once frightened him as a boy, and sees something there that he has never seen before. Not fear. Longing.

"You hear it too," he says.

"The word." Qin Hao glances at his hands. "At night, I hear it. Cole. Not as a name. As a call. Like a man shouting down a well." His voice is rough. "I do not know why. I only know that when you opened your door, it stopped, and when you closed it, it began again, and I have thought I am going mad."

"You are not going mad."

"Then what?"

"I think," Jian says carefully, "that the Gate has been calling an Operator for a very long time. And I think it calls everyone who stood close to the wall when the last one came."

Qin Hao is silent. Then he laughs, a short ugly bark, and shakes his head.

"Well. I have been called by worse." He pushes off the wall, heavy and slow. "Go to bed, boy. You look like a dead man. Whatever you decide, decide it with sleep in you."

* * *

Yue is sitting on the Garden Hall's back step when he comes in, with Pebble in her lap and a blanket round her shoulders.

She is twenty-three, small and dark and quiet, with their mother's narrow hands and none of the rest of the family's reserve. She has no spiritual root. The Mirror at the Sect's gate looked at her when she was fifteen and showed nothing at all, and she nodded politely and went home and began, that same week, to keep a ledger of every door in the Garden that did not close quite right. It is a thick book now. Wenyuan calls it her scripture.

"You have been to the stair," she says, without turning.

"Yes."

"They asked you something."

Jian sits down on the step beside her. The night air is sharp enough to sting. "How do you know?"

"Pebble told me you would come back looking like that." She strokes the small gray head. "She says the seams are loud tonight. All of them. She says there is a very long one under the Dock, and thirty-one little ones hanging from it like beads." She is quiet for a moment. "She says one of the beads is going dim."

"Yes."

"Which one?"

"The ninth."

Yue nods slowly, as though a sum has come out as she expected. "I thought so. I have been hearing someone breathe at the bottom of the well for a month. I thought it was my ear." She draws the blanket tighter. "Are you going to wake them?"

"I do not know."

"You do not like it."

"I do not trust it."

"Is that the same?"

He looks at his sister, at the plain, serious profile in the starlight, and thinks that of all the people who might have asked, she is the one he would least like to lie to.

"No," he says. "It is not the same. I want to do it. That is the trouble. I want very much to do it, and a thing that is built to be wanted that badly has usually been built by someone who knew I would."

"Then ask the one who built it."

"I cannot."

"Ask the one who wrote the note." She says it as simply as she says everything. "Ethan Cole. He said bring someone who hears seams. You brought me. So ask him what I am for."

Pebble lifts her head. In the dark her eyes are two dull coins.

"He is not far," says the little beast in her clear child's voice. "He is under the stone. He has been under the stone the whole time."

Nobody says anything for a very long while.

"Not tonight," Jian says finally.

"Not tonight," Yue agrees. She leans her head on his shoulder, lightly, as she did when she was six. "But soon. I would like to meet him. I have a great many questions about his handwriting."

* * *

Bai receives him at the first gray hour, in the stone-floored infirmary behind the Pill Hall, with a cup of something bitter and his sleeves rolled.

He is eighty-one now. His back has curved into a question mark, his white hair stands up in tufts, and his hands, the long, spotted, infinitely careful hands that once taught Jian to read a pulse, tremble when he holds them out. But the eyes behind the thick lenses are exactly what they were. Quick. Merciless. Interested.

"Thirty-one," he says, when Jian has told him. "Held by a rope. One failing at a rate of, what, a year of breath per season?"

"They said twenty years left in the weakest. They did not say how it was measured."

"No. They would not." Bai pours the cup into a basin, reconsiders, pours another. "Show me the Roll."

"It is in Ye's stick."

"Then show me where it touched you." He holds out his hand for Jian's wrist, closes his fingers, and goes very still, in the way he does when he is listening to a river at the bottom of a canyon. A minute passes. Two. When he opens his eyes, the lenses have fogged.

"There is a draw on you," he says slowly. "Very fine. A thread. It runs from your breastbone down into the floor. I do not think it is taking anything yet. I think it is measuring."

"Measuring what?"

"How much you could give." Bai lets go and sits back heavily. "Boy, I have spent seventy years studying what a body can lose and keep living. Everything has a floor. A man can lose a limb, a lung, a year, a name. What he cannot lose is the thing that decides which of those he is willing to lose. That is a Keeper's gift. It is also a Keeper's curse. The Roll is not asking if you will do it. It is asking what it would cost you to refuse."

"I already know that."

"Do you?" The old man's smile is dry. "A Keeper's price for refusal is paid in nights. Every night you decline, a little more of your sleep goes to the Chain. Not all. Enough that you will feel it in a month and hate it in a year. They do not need to threaten you, because you have already offered."

Jian says nothing.

"I can help," says Bai. "A little. There is a root, the nine-year Heartroot Qinghe grows at the back of the Garden. Steeped with white moss and a little river silt, it slows a draw. Not stops it. Slows. Four years, five if I am clever. I could send a dose each season to the sleeping hall, and the ninth would last."

"What does it cost?"

"Ten roots a season, and one of my afternoons." Bai lifts a finger. "And the Garden's seed stock for the Heartroot, because I must have the fresh crown, not the dried. Qinghe will bleat. She will give it anyway."

"Then do it."

"I intended to." The old man picks up his cup, drinks, grimaces. "But you should know that a stopgap is an admission. If I steep this for five years, and you have not decided by then, you will have decided."

"I know."

"I thought you did." He puts the cup down. "Go and sleep. You look like something a cat left on the step."

Jian bows. At the door, the old man's voice stops him.

"Lin Jian."

"Yes?"

"Whatever you do with the third stone," says Bai, without looking up from his basin, "do it in daylight, with your family in the room. I have watched a great many men decide great things alone at midnight. I have buried most of them."

* * *

Sleep does not come. He lies in the Garden Hall's narrow back room, in the bed he has slept in since he was a child, and listens to the house breathe.

It is a good house. It is warm and crooked and smells of wood-smoke and boiled grain. Through the wall he can hear Feng's soft, regular snore, and further off the tap of a spoon against a bowl as Qinghe, unable to sleep either, sets out the morning porridge. Somewhere in the dark, Pebble is curled on Yue's bed, murmuring in her sleep. It is, he thinks, the most completely defended place in the world, and he would die for every board of it.

And under all of it, under the floor, under the rock, under the Dock he cannot see, thirty-one people are breathing in the same slow rhythm, and one of them has twenty years.

Nineteen, he thinks. We are not precise.

He turns on his side. He thinks of the stone in his pocket, cold as a coin. He thinks of Lan Tong, who refused to speak. He thinks of Ethan Cole's handwriting, blue and cramped and tired: Do not go through. He thinks of the first stone and the second, and of how neatly each had fitted its socket, as though the Dock had been waiting for it.

It has your name on its seam.

The Operator before him wrote, ask where the Operators went. He has asked. The Chain has answered: the eighth. It has not said what became of the first seven.

At last, toward dawn, he gets up and sits at the little desk by the window, in the gray, and takes out a sheet of paper. He writes two columns. In the left, he lists what he knows. In the right, what he does not.

The left column is short.

The right column runs off the page.

At the bottom, in his own plain hand, he writes one line, and looks at it for a long time.

Wait. But not forever.

He does not know how long forever is. He only knows, with the quiet, absolute certainty of a man who has made a choice that will cost him sleep for twenty years, that he has just decided to let thirty-one people go on dreaming for as long as it takes him to find out who built the trap.

And that somewhere below, in the dark, a ninth sleeper has begun, ever so slightly, to count.
